sources.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways

items.title: Ukraine Moves to Shield Its Railways as Strikes on the Network Intensify
items.body:
Ukraine's government has asked for outside help replacing destroyed locomotives and is drawing up plans to keep passengers safe, as Russia steps up attacks on the country's rail infrastructure. Railways have carried much of Ukraine's wartime passenger and freight traffic, which is why the locomotives are the sort of asset that gets counted in public.

The two things Kyiv is asking for are different kinds of problem: rolling stock is a procurement question, passenger safety is an operating one. Neither is solved by rebuilding track alone.

sources.title: 'Insufficient funds' to pay Brewdog creditors after takeover deal

items.title: Brewdog Administrators Say the Money Isn't There for Creditors
items.body:
Administrators handling Brewdog after its takeover say about £489,000 was owed for staff wages and holiday pay, and £2.4 million was owed to HMRC for unpaid VAT — amounts they describe as insufficient funds to pay out. That is the plain sequence of an insolvency: wages and tax arrears sit at the front of the queue, and the question is whether the estate covers them at all.

The wage figure and the VAT figure together are a useful reminder of how quickly a company's obligations outrun the cash in the room.

sources.title: Flight chaos caused by 'millisecond' software defect, report says

items.title: A Software Defect Measured in Milliseconds Grounded More Than 2,000 Flights
items.body:
A report into a major flight disruption traces the failure to a software defect lasting milliseconds. The consequence was more than 2,000 cancelled flights and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected.

That ratio is the interesting part: the fault itself was brief, the outage was not. Systems built to fail fast and restart can still cascade if the restart is shared.

sources.title: Canada and EU: A look at the bloc's special relationships

items.title: What an Associate Membership Would Actually Be
items.body:
Talk of Canada taking some form of associate membership in the European Union raises a prior question: what is the template? The EU already has particular arrangements with individual countries — different tiers of closeness, not one membership product with a flag on it.

Geography is not the obstacle here. The distance between Canada and Europe is noted and set aside in the same breath as the political ties being discussed.

So the useful way to read any associate-membership proposal is to ask which existing arrangement it most resembles, and which obligations come with that shape. "Associate" is a category, not a single status.

sources.title: The new lines of southern Lebanon

items.title: A Monitoring Mandate Younger Than the Group It Watches
items.body: Twenty years ago the United Nations widened the mandate of its force in southern Lebanon so that it would monitor adherence to a ceasefire in the fighting between Israel and Lebanon's Hezbollah. That is a narrow, specific job: watch whether a truce holds. The monitoring role was an expansion of the force's remit, tied to a particular ceasefire rather than to peacekeeping in general, and NPR reports that the mandate now runs to checking compliance with it. Hezbollah is considerably older than that job description. It is Iran-backed, and NPR describes it as the militant group created in 1982 to counter a second Israeli invasion of Lebanon. The mandate is therefore decades younger than the organisation it was written to watch — a gap worth keeping in mind whenever a ceasefire is described as monitored.

sources.title: Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic”

discussion.body: Treating post as the part of production worth anchoring is a real choice: edit suites don't need weather, a coastline, or a friendly mayor.
Once a state starts choosing which stages of production to subsidise, the boundary is a policy decision rather than an economic one. The same logic could justify anchoring any stage.

items.title: A California Bill Aimed at the Edit, Not the Shoot
items.body: The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising a California bill that offers tax incentives to productions that shoot outside the state — provided they bring their post-production work to California. That inverts the usual location logic. Instead of chasing the shoot itself, the crews and the months on location, the incentive chases the finishing rooms and tries to make the edit the last stage that stays home. Whether finishing houses follow a tax code the way productions have followed one out of state is the bet being placed.

sources.title: There might be no economic case for expanding the Port of Churchill, but that may not be the point

items.title: A $3-Billion Port Expansion Argued in the Language of Sovereignty
items.body: A port expansion and railway upgrade on Hudson Bay carries a $3-billion price tag, and the case for it has been made in a different currency than traffic forecasts: a Hudson Bay shipping route, the framing goes, is essential for Canadian sovereignty. That is what makes the question CBC puts to Manitobans so pointed — why aren't Canada and Manitoba simply proceeding? Once sovereignty is the stated reason, the ordinary commercial test is no longer the thing doing the deciding. And a project described as essential that still isn't simply under way leaves the strategic argument carrying the whole load.

sources.title: Michigan city defends itself against accusations of favoring Muslim holidays over other faiths

items.title: A Detroit Suburb Is Sued Over Which Holidays It Pays to Mark
items.body: A lawsuit filed Thursday accuses a Detroit suburb and its mayor of spending thousands of dollars to celebrate Muslim holidays while ignoring Christian and Jewish holidays. The city issued a statement in response, delivered by a spokesperson. Note what each half of that exchange is: the spending claim is an allegation made in a legal filing, and the city's answer is a statement rather than a ruling. The dispute runs on money and recognition at once — which holidays a municipality marks with public funds, and which it doesn't.

sources.title: Trump announces all 50 states joining Medicaid drug pricing model

discussion.body: “GENEROUS” is a label, not evidence. Naming a model is the easy part; publishing the deal terms is what would let anyone check whether billions actually move.

Negotiated drug deals can be genuinely secret and still save money — bargaining power sometimes depends on not broadcasting terms. The finding is that the savings are unclear to outsiders, not that they are absent.
Fair, but “trust us, and also we won't show you” is a hard pitch to sustain past the announcement. The number either shows up in Medicaid's books or it doesn't.

items.title: A Medicaid drug-pricing plan whose billions are claimed, not shown
items.body: The Trump administration claims Medicaid will save billions on prescription drug costs through a plan it calls the Medicaid “GENEROUS” model, according to PBS NewsHour. Experts say the savings are unclear, because the content of the deals behind the plan isn't public. That is the whole shape of the claim so far: a large number on one side, and no inspectable arithmetic on the other. A savings figure is only as strong as the contracts it rests on, and those contracts, as reported, haven't been disclosed.

sources.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters denied access to White House following Trump ban

discussion.body: Banning outlets by name makes White House access look less like a shared press facility and more like a license the occupant can revoke.
A denied seat still isn't a silenced newsroom — those organizations keep reporting from outside the grounds. Access is a convenience and a signal, not a switch that turns coverage off.

items.title: Three reporters blocked from the White House grounds after their outlets were banned
items.body: Three reporters were blocked from the White House grounds on Saturday morning, NPR reports, a day after President Trump said CNN, Politico and MS NOW would be banned for reporting what he called “FICTION and LIES.” The ban was framed as a judgment on coverage; turning reporters away at the gate is what it looks like on the ground. The unresolved question is what the ban means in practice for those outlets' access — a single morning's exclusion, or the start of a standing arrangement.

sources.title: ‘Possible Love’: The Cast Of Lee Chang-Dong’s Venice Award-Winner Discuss Its Themes Of Class Division – TIFF Studio

items.title: Lee Chang-dong returns with two marriages and a documentary crew
items.body: “Possible Love” is Lee Chang-dong's first film in eight years, and its premise is a collision of two marriages: a laid-off worker and his wife, and a documentary filmmaker and her husband, whose paths cross during the making of a documentary. Lee wrote it with Oh Jung-mi, and Netflix is distributing. A camera crew is a useful device for this kind of story — someone is always deciding what to point at and what to leave out, and marriage is where that editing instinct gets ugly.

sources.title: If most Albertans don't want to leave Canada, where is the pro-Canada movement?

discussion.body: Fundraising and online chatter select for intensity, not headcount. A movement can look enormous precisely because its supporters are the ones who show up, donate and post.
And yet intensity is what turns out on the day that matters. A quiet majority that stays home loses to a loud minority that doesn't, whatever the polls said the week before.
True, but that's an argument about turnout, not about support. The reported pattern is still a mismatch between what most people say and who is making the noise.

items.title: Most Albertans oppose separation. Fundraising and online chatter tell a different story
items.body: Over the last year, polling has found again and again that most Albertans oppose separation, CBC reports — yet fundraising and online chatter would leave a different impression. That gap between a polling majority and the noise around a movement is worth noticing on its own terms. Intensity and volume are not the same as numbers, and the things that are easy to see are not always the things that are numerous. Which of the two actually decides a vote is the interesting question, and not one a poll answers by itself.

sources.title: Canada’s defence minister calls U.S. deal on Greenland ‘encouraging’

items.title: Canada's defence minister calls the US–Greenland deal 'encouraging'
items.body: National Defence Minister David McGuinty calls the United States' deal to boost its military presence in Greenland 'encouraging.' The arrangement splits presence from sovereignty: Washington gets the expanded military footprint, Denmark keeps control of the island. One word of approval is a verdict on a bargain between two other governments rather than a policy Canada has signed up to, and 'encouraging' is the sort of adjective that leaves the specifics for later.

sources.title: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’

items.title: The Scream poster that left Henry Winkler's name off
items.body: Henry Winkler, the Happy Days star, played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original Scream, the film that went on to become one of horror's most successful franchises. Variety reports that learning his name would not be used on the poster wasn't one of his happier days — while his character's entrance drew applause during screen tests. Screen-test applause and a poster credit measure different things: one is a room's reaction on the night, the other a marketing judgment about what belongs on a wall.

sources.title: Playful Provocation: Hypermediacy in Mario Bava’s Danger: Diabolik

discussion.body: A decoy opening is ordinary heist grammar: hide the loot in the first act so the reveal has somewhere to land. It doesn't have to mean anything about the film's surfaces.
The interesting part is who runs the trick. The empty convoy is the inspector's scheme rather than the thief's, so the film's first deception comes from the side the audience assumes is honest.

items.title: Danger: Diabolik opens with a heist that is actually a decoy
items.body: Danger: Diabolik opens with a heist that isn't one. Inspector Ginko (Michel Piccoli) has arranged a spectacular motorcade to transport a large sum of banknotes; the convoy, it turns out, is carrying no banknotes at all. It is a diversion, and it is the inspector's diversion — the film's first elaborate deception is mounted by the side we expect to be straight with us. Senses of Cinema's essay on the film calls the opening an elaborate ploy, a project of misdirection, which is a tidy way to teach an audience to watch the con rather than the loot.

sources.title: John Wilson on ‘The History of Concrete’ and What’s Wrong With the Documentary Space: ‘People Are Retelling Stories That Have Already Happened’

items.title: A documentary about concrete — and about selling a documentary about concrete
items.body: John Wilson's new documentary is called The History of Concrete and, as Variety notes, is about the history of concrete. It is also about selling a documentary titled The History of Concrete, a job the film treats as almost as hard as the material itself. It is in theaters now. A subject that ordinary turns out to be a marketing problem, and the film's own pitch becomes part of its subject.

sources.title: 2 sudden deaths prompt public safety warning from Halifax police

items.title: Halifax Police Issue Public Safety Warning After Two Sudden Deaths and a Third Person in Distress
items.body: Halifax Regional Police issued a public safety warning after two sudden deaths and a person found in serious medical distress, all within a 24-hour period. The warning covers three incidents in a single day — a cluster that police evidently judged significant enough to alert the public rather than treat as isolated cases.

sources.title: Rabid Dogs

discussion.body: The auteur case and the commercial case are separate arguments. A box set proves there's a market for lurid covers and cheap rights — not that the films are good.
Worldwide retrospectives aren't something a distributor can manufacture. Programmers stake their institutional credibility on the filmmakers they revive.
Both things can be true: the films merit the retrospectives, and the umbrella collection exists mostly because the catalogue was available and the artwork sells.

items.title: Bava Is an Auteur, and His Work Is Also a Home-Entertainment Goldmine
items.body:
Mario Bava's passionate fans have no doubt about his status as a major auteur. He is also, per one film journal, one of the few named filmmakers whose work "guarantee[s] huge sales in new home entertainment formats," promoted under umbrella collections, shown at retrospectives worldwide.

Critic: The auteur reading and the box-set economy are two entirely separate arguments, and the second one keeps getting smuggled in as evidence for the first.
Fan: Or maybe the box sets exist because the auteur reading is correct. Nobody builds a "Bava Collection" around a hack.
Critic: Nobody builds one around a neglected genius either, unless the rights are cheap and the artwork is lurid. That's a distribution fact, not a verdict.
Fan: The retrospectives aren't distribution. Those are programmers staking reputations.
Critic: Fair. But "major auteur" and "sells well on Blu-ray" are not the same claim, and only one of them is settled by a sales chart.

sources.title: Cosmic amnesia

discussion.body: The bell analogy is useful because it separates the ringing from the silence. The interesting question isn't the oscillation, it's what the settling state retains.
Calling it "forgetting" already smuggles in an answer. A system can lose accessible information without losing information full stop — those are different claims.
True, and the framing here is deliberately provocative. "Rings then settles into silence" is the physical description; "forgetting" is the interpretation laid on top of it.

items.title: Why a Black Hole Forgets: The Ringdown and the Information It Loses
items.body:
A black hole rings like a struck bell, then settles into silence — forgetting almost everything about its history. That is the puzzle Aeon poses: why does a gravitational system that formed from a specific, violent, detailed collapse end in a state that seems to retain only a few properties?

The bell analogy is doing real work. A struck bell's ring encodes the strike: how hard, where, at what angle. As the vibration damps out, the sound stops carrying that information. A black hole's ringdown works similarly — the oscillation dies away, and what remains is characterised by mass, spin and charge rather than the particulars of what fell in. The question of where the rest of the information went is the whole game.

sources.title: Maxxing treats life as a problem when it’s a mystery

items.title: Marcel's Distinction: A Problem You Solve vs. a Mystery You Enter
items.body:
Gabriel Marcel drew a distinction that is easy to state and hard to hold onto: a problem is something I confront, something outside me that I can survey, solve, and put down. A mystery is something I am inside of — my participation is part of the thing being examined, so I can't get the clean outside vantage that problem-solving requires.

Psyche frames this as an antidote to what it calls maxxing culture, the impulse to treat existence as a malfunction to be optimised. The Marcel move isn't to give up on improvement; it's to notice that some questions change when you stand inside them, and that treating them as fixable objects may be the error. As the essay puts it: don't fix existence, be open to it.
